A recent trip to Poland by its founder and president is a prime example of what the relatively new Coalfields and Cobblestones is all about. Blake Moss founded the nonprofit organization in July 2025, shortly after returning from his first visit to Poland. After coming home from his second trip in May of this year, Moss had already put his words into action. "I'm trying to connect Appalachia with the rest of the world," Moss said in explaining the organization's purpose. "I believe that our comparative advantage, which is the thing that we're best at compared to the rest of the world, is developing relationships. I think our people have a lot of potential, and I think that potential can be unleashed by developing relationships with the world." Moss is a public administration specialist for the Big Sandy Area Development District, but he is quick to point out that the ADD and Coalfields and Cobblestones are separate entities that are not associated with each other. In 2025, Moss said he was "getting fed up with my life in Eastern Kentucky" and looking for other jobs outside the Big Sandy Region. To get away from his frustration and stress, Moss decided to take a trip to Poland. The excursion changed his life, he said. "It completely transformed me as a person, and it completely transformed how I see this place," Moss said. "I went there, and the people were just so friendly, and everyone was so interested in America and wanted to connect. I saw so many things that I wanted to bring back home." He founded Coalfields and Cobblestones a month after returning home. Moss demonstrated the purpose of the organization when he returned to Poland in May. "During my two weeks in Silesia, Poland, my first few days there, I met with a young lady who is a college graduate, and she studies cognitive science, which is essentially like an AI-related tech field," he said. "She's been looking for fellowships in New York City and Los Angeles, and has not received anything, has not heard anything back. I showed her Bit Source, a local tech company in Pikeville. She said she was interested. We were able to work out a fellowship, so in September she'll be coming to Pikeville for a fellowship with Bit Source. This is a microcosm of what Coalfields and Cobblestones can become. More than just fellowships, but bringing in engineers, artists, businesses by cutting out the middleman and making things person to person. Really, this is grassroots diplomacy. Diplomacy is connecting countries; I'm connecting people in countries." Moss said Silesia is known as the historic coal-mining capital of Europe. "A very interesting thing about their mines is each mine in Poland has a chamber of heritage that keeps track of the mine's history throughout the mine's operation," he said. "When that mine closes, they don't have to scramble to get everything together. It's already been keeping track, and they will usually take all that history and give it up to a central entity, who then digitizes it and stores it and displays it." Moss said he met with several institutions that had to do with cultural preservation and historical preservation. "I realized that we have a lot we can learn from them in that regard," he said. "And there's also a lot they can learn from us. The main thing I see there is, in 2049, all mining in the European Union has to stop. It's European Union mandate. Poland's in the European Union, and in the Silesian Region, they have 100,000 people that work in mining or mining adjacent industries, industries supported by mining. They're not all miners. As you know, for every one miner, you have two people to support that miner. Mining-connected industry is a huge economic driver, and right now the main thing they're doing is severance packages for people who retire and things like that. That doesn't give anybody a purpose. One thing we've done very well here is through things like eKAMI, the community colleges, we're extremely good at upscaling workers and at finding people a new purpose. Unfortunately, those purposes are not always here in the region. They sometimes have to go other places to get jobs, but nonetheless, we're very skilled at that." https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyl.text: Figure caption, Hikers airlifted to safety after flash floods hit Grand Canyon trail By Madeline Halpert ,Â Brandon Drenon Â and Â Darren Bett ,Â lead weather presenter Published 30 August 2026 Updated 6 hours ago Two people have died and 14 remain missing or unaccounted for after flash flooding swept through parts of the Grand Canyon, the National Park Service (NPS) has said. The flood hit Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area on Saturday afternoon, wiping out footbridges and propelling boulders downstream. The body of a 46-year-old man was found on Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, the park service said. Sixty-two people have so far been airlifted out of the area. "The whole thing was terrifying," said Nikki Baggs, 41, who was among those to be airlifted out of the bottom of the Grand Canyon with her two friends. "It was a beautiful day and then people were screaming, running," she told the BBC. Baggs said she and her friends had just dropped off their belongings at a cabin in Phantom Ranch - a remote lodge at the bottom of the Grand Canyon - when they decided to venture out to enjoy the nice day. Before they knew it, a flood of water was sweeping through the area. As soon as the rain hit, Baggs and her friends headed toward higher ground, where they sat at a picnic table, before rangers yelled to them to run again to a different ledge, where they waited with others for hours before they were evacuated at around 21:30 local time (04:30 GMT). Baggs said she and her two friends had been looking forward to a steak dinner at Phantom Ranch - but were now just grateful to be alive thanks to a swift response from park rangers. "It was a really uniquely co-ordinated effort," she said. "That's what made us feel safe about all of it in an unsafe situation." Baggs said she and her friends watched from higher ground as bridges were swept away. Image source, Nikki Baggs Image caption, Nikki Baggs posed for this photo just before the rain hit In a statement on Monday, the NPS said search and rescue efforts continue. The recent rains in the Grand Canyon area, and more widely in south-western parts of the US, are due to monsoonal showers. A change in wind direction at this time of year pulls warm, moist air northward from the Gulf of California and the tropical Pacific, triggering storms over mountainous terrain. The storms are difficult to pinpoint in forecasts and so can strike without warning. But because the ground is usually very dry, any heavy downpours lead to dangerous flash flooding and frequent lightning which increases the threat of wildfires. Flood watches from the National Weather Service cover large parts of Arizona, as well as New Mexico, Utah and Colorado. There are lots of showers currently showing on the weather radar and these downpours will continue during Monday. The threat of flooding is something that will remain for many more weeks. The North American monsoon season usually runs to the end of September. Joey Martin told the BBC that he was at the Grand Canyon working on a transcanyon pipeline project when dense, grey clouds rolled in. He described rain "coming down so hard and so thick that you couldn't see the Grand Canyon walls". "You couldn't see anything," Martin said. Visibility returned roughly 30 minutes later, he said. That's when he saw the creek begin to rise. It eventually turned into a torrent of mud and debris that slammed into a nearby bridge connecting Martin's work site to his living quarters. "From where we were standing, it looked to be about 15ft tall," he said. "That wall of debris ended up taking out the bridge right there." Martin said he and roughly 16 other workers were there and coordinated with NPS once it became clear conditions were unsafe. They gathered hikers in the area and headed for higher ground. Eventually all were airlifted out. "It was scary," he recalled. "Never been in any kind of vicinity of something like that to that caliber," he said. "Staying calm was hard, but everybody kind of played a part in keeping people calm and keeping people, you know, focused on just getting away from the danger." The NPS initially said it was looking for information about 15 people who were thought to be missing or unaccounted for. It reported that flooding had caused significant damage in some areas and that trails in the area have been closed. Overnight guest lodgings in the South Rim will be stopped from Monday until further notice as the floods have caused "extensive damage" to the national park's water infrastructure. On Monday, the NPS said that preliminary assessments indicate about 40% of the Transcanyon Waterline, which delivers water for visitors and approximately 2,500 residents, was damaged or destroyed in the flood. The NPS asked anyone who knew of hikers or backpackers who were in the inner canyon along the Bright Angel Creek corridor on Saturday to get in touch. Image source, Grand Canyon National Park Image caption, The Grand Canyon National Park posted this image on Facebook while warning footbridges had been destroyed by the flooding The NPS also warned that more thunderstorms and heavy rainfall were forecast for Monday, which could lead to "additional flash flooding, debris flows, rockfall and changing trail and river conditions". The Grand Canyon is one of the most popular national parks in the US, with about five million people visiting each year. The Bright Angel trail is its most popular hike. https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: FORT WORTH, Texas — Germany received its first F-35 jet on Friday but the collapse of Europe's flagship next-generation fighter project is forcing Berlin to rethink what will follow the U.S.-built jet. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius was in Texas at the Lockheed Martin factory for the ceremony. The delivery of the fighter jet was long-planned, but the death of the Franco-German-Spanish Future Combat Air System fighter jet development program earlier this year is fueling calls in Berlin to expand the initial €10 billion order of 35 American jets. The Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II is supposed to solve Germany's immediate problem: replacing its aging Tornado fighter-bombers and preserving its role in NATO nuclear sharing while Europe developed its own next-generation fighter. Advertisement Advertisement But without the FCAS, Berlin is left without an obvious European successor. “We want and need to maintain nuclear sharing,” Pistorius said ahead of the handover. The F-35, he argued, is currently “the only aircraft in the world” capable of fulfilling that mission. Under the NATO nuclear-sharing program, Germany and other select allies have aircraft that can carry U.S. nuclear bombs, although the decision to use them remains with Washington. The first F-35s will remain in the United States for training, with German pilots and technicians preparing for operations before more jets are sent to Büchel in late 2027. Full operational capability is expected by 2030. Berlin currently operates around 80 Tornados, and some missions will migrate to the Eurofighter Typhoon. But the collapse of FCAS has opened a longer-term gap in Germany's plans for its combat-air fleet. During June's Berlin Air Show, Pistorius said Berlin is weighing whether to acquire additional F-35s as a “bridge” option after the FCAS failure, to join an existing international sixth-generation program or to develop a national effort headed by Airbus. Advertisement Advertisement German Air Force Chief Lt. Gen. Holger Neumann said at the show that he has asked the defense ministry to procure “fifth-gen-plus platforms beyond 2035,” adding: “I’m not saying the new system has to be ready [in 2035], but we have to pick up there.” One option is for Germany to boost the number of F-35s in its fleet by buying 15 additional jets. “The F-35 has a clear mission in nuclear sharing,” said Marie-Christine von Hahn, managing director of Germany’s aerospace and defense industry association BDLI. But she warned that the procurement should not distract policymakers from a larger challenge. “Europe’s air forces need their own wings,” she said. “In Germany in particular, we must continue to be capable of developing, building, maintaining and upgrading combat aircraft ourselves.” FCAS troubles The fighter component of FCAS collapsed due to fights over control between the leading French and German companies involved in the project. Paris and Berlin also clashed over the role of the fighter, with France pushing for a lighter jet able to land on its aircraft carrier while Germany wanted a heavier one for air-superiority roles. Germany is also looking at the U.K.-Italian-Japanese Global Combat Air Programme, although the current members are not keen on expanding the number of partners. Advertisement Advertisement Then there's the future sixth-generation U.S. F-47 under development by Boeing, which could go into service by the end of the decade. However, U.S. President Donald Trump has said the U.S. will sell less capable versions to its allies, undercutting their attractiveness. While a sixth-generation aircraft remains a long-term goal, for German industry the crucial question is how deeply domestic companies will be integrated into the maintenance and future support structure of the F-35. Lockheed Martin says that about a quarter of the jet's components are made in Europe. Germany's Rheinmetall is making fuselage parts to be supplied to foreign customers. That makes the F-35 a product of the close defense-industrial ties linking Europe, Canada and the U.S. — ties now being tested by doubts over Washington's commitment to European defense under Trump. Pistorius underlined that those links still matter to German defense. “Whenever we talk about independence,” he said, “we must also recognize that there are mutual dependencies that keep allies close and allow them to benefit from one another.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/09/27/svaj.text: Menü Kereső Leszavazták a svájciak, hogy az alkotmányban írják elő a szigorúbb semlegességi politikát Külföld Krász Zsombor Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom A Svájcban a vasárnap tartott népszavazáson a résztvevők több mint 70 százaléka elutasította, hogy az ország politikai semlegességének szigorúbb értelmezését rögzítsék az alkotmányban – írta meg a Swissinfo, miután a gsf.bern közvélemény-kutató cég egyik vezetője a svájci SRF csatornán közölte az előzetes eredményeket. A kutató szerint a többség egyértelműen úgy gondolja, hogy a parlamentnek és a kormánynak „mozgásteret” kell hagyni a semlegességi politika kialakításában, ahelyett, hogy azt egy véglegesen alkotmányos meghatározáshoz kötnék. A részvételi arány 47 százalék volt. A kezdeményezést a nemzeti konzervatív Svájci Néppárthoz közeli Pro Schweiz csoport indította, és a népszavazás középpontba hozta azokat a svájci vitákat, amiket Oroszország Ukrajna elleni 2022-es inváziója indított. Ilyen vita például, hogy Svájc átvette az Európai Unió Moszkvával szemben bevezetett szankcióit. A kezdeményezők szerint a szankciók átvételével felhígult Svájc hagyományos, neutrális álláspontja, és ez nem szolgálta Svájc érdekeit, így azt akarták elérni, hogy a jövőben ne vezethessenek be hasonló szankciókat, csak akkor, ha azokat az ENSZ Biztonsági Tanácsa jóváhagyja. A semlegesség fogalmának alkotmányos meghatározása mellett a szövetségesekkel, így a NATO-val folytatott együttműködést is korlátozta volna az ország vezetésének. Marianne Binder-Keller, a Közép Párt szenátora szerint a kezdeményezés „teljes elszigeteltségbe” sodorta volna Svájcot az új biztonsági kihívások idején, és az eredmény azt jelzi, Svájc „a nyugati, szabályokon alapuló biztonsági rendszer része, együttműködési partner, és részt vesz a szankciókban”, ha arra nemzetközi jogsértések miatt van szükség. A Pro Schweiznak egyébként sem volt könnyű dolga: ugyan bőséges finanszírozást kaptak a kampányhoz, csak egy nagy politikai csoport, a jobboldali Svájci Néppárt támogatta a javaslatot. A Swissinfo szerint az sem segíthette az ügyet, hogy a választók úgy gondolták, oroszbarát volt a kezdeményezés, és a mellette kampányoló korábbi néppárti vezető, Christoph Blocher saját üzleti érdekeit szolgálná. Egy másik kérdésben is szavaztak a svájciak: a hazai termesztés ösztönzésével egy évtized alatt 46 százalékról 70 százalékra akarták emelni Svájc önellátását az élelmiszer-termelés területén. Ez a kezdeményezés azonban szintén elbukott, a résztvevők közel 73 százaléka ellene szavazott. Utóbbi döntést még nagyrészt a gazdák is elutasították, és sokan attól tartottak, hogy ezzel a hús- és tejfogyasztási lehetőségeiket szűkítenék.
